I ran one small random circuit sampling job on IQM's free Garnet test device, garnet:mock. It used 1000 shots and cost no credits. The job ID is 01a16041-8c95-7595-8f93-c2815faa19db, and it finished with status DONE.

The circuit:
- It used 8 qubits that form a connected chain on Garnet: QB1, QB2, QB5, QB4, QB3, QB8, QB9 and QB10.
- It had 8 layers of two-qubit CZ gates in a brickwork pattern, 28 CZ gates in total.
- Before each layer, every qubit got a random half-turn rotation (square root of X, Y or W), and one more random layer came after the last CZ layer.
- After compiling, the circuit had 64 single-qubit gates, 28 CZ gates and 8 measurements.

How the score works:
- I computed the exact output probability of all 256 possible 8-bit results on my laptop.
- Linear XEB is 256 times the average ideal probability of the results the machine returned, minus 1.
- A score near 0 means the results are no better than random guessing.
- The ideal score for this circuit is 0.883. That is what a perfect, noise-free quantum computer would get on average. I drew 1000 samples from the exact distribution as a check, and they scored 0.873.
- Real hardware lands between 0 and the ideal score. Each error pulls the score toward 0, so the score also estimates how often the whole circuit ran without an error.

The result: xeb_measured is 0.543. Do not read this number as hardware quality. The mock device does not run the circuit. It returned only 8 different bitstrings, each about 125 times, which is a fixed test pattern. A real random circuit spreads its results over many of the 256 bitstrings. The 0.543 only reflects that a few of those test bitstrings happen to be likely for this circuit. The run checks that the circuit, the job and the scoring all work. A run on real Garnet would cost a small number of credits and would give a real score, probably well below 0.883 because of noise.

Why 8 qubits is easy for a laptop but 50 or more is not:
- To score or imitate the samples, a classical computer must track 2 to the power n numbers.
- For 8 qubits that is 256 numbers. My laptop did it in well under a second.
- For 50 qubits it is about 10 to the power 15 numbers, which takes petabytes of memory.
- Each added qubit doubles the work. Around 50 to 70 qubits with enough layers, the best supercomputer methods would need years or more.

The principle: a random quantum circuit spreads its output over an exponentially large set of results in a very uneven pattern. A quantum computer produces samples from that pattern directly. A classical computer has to calculate it. XEB measures how closely the samples follow the true pattern. Google and others used this test at 53 or more qubits to claim quantum advantage. At that size the score can no longer be checked exactly, so they relied on checks done at smaller sizes.

The script is /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-34/rcs_xeb.py. The saved counts and scores are in /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-34/rcs_result.json.
